tagline.text: Camarines Norte's highest peak, a two-day jungle volcano trek

location.label: Location
location.text: Around San Lorenzo Ruiz and Labo, Camarines Norte

best_season.label: Best time to visit
best_season.text: March–May dry season (June–November brings rain, leeches and swollen rivers)

duration.label: Time needed
duration.text: 2 days, 1 night (a day hike takes 10–12 hours)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱2,500~5,000 (per person, excluding round-trip transport from Manila, with guide and vehicle costs shared)

airport.label: Nearest airport
airport.text: Naga Airport (WNP) or overland from Manila

children.text: Mount Labo is a potentially active volcano 1,544 m high that straddles Camarines Norte, Camarines Sur and Quezon, and it is the highest peak in Camarines Norte. It is known for a two-day jungle trek along an old geothermal exploration road, across rivers and through mossy forest.

Mount Labo is a stratovolcano rising at the northwestern tip of the Bicol Peninsula on Luzon, on the border of Camarines Norte, Camarines Sur and Quezon. The summit lies in Camarines Norte at about 1,544 m above sea level. The volcano is huge, with a base roughly 35 km wide, and it is made of andesite and dacite rock. The current cone formed about 270,000 years ago, and the last known activity was pyroclastic flows about 27,000 years ago. The Philippine Institute of Volcanology and Seismology (PHIVOLCS) classifies it as potentially active, and the mountain has hot springs and hydrothermal areas that led to geothermal exploration in the past.

For travelers, Mount Labo is a place to walk through jungle, not to look into a crater. The roughly 13 km from the trailhead to the campsite follows an old road cut during geothermal exploration, now overgrown and rough. You cross the rivers several times along this stretch. Past the campsite the trail narrows and climbs a steep forest path of moss, roots and wet rock all the way to the summit. Local guides look after the hard-to-follow sections and show the way. Most of the route needs no technical climbing, but the distance, humidity and leeches mean you need good fitness and preparation.

Most people take a night bus from Manila to Daet, eat breakfast, and ride to Barangay San Isidro in San Lorenzo Ruiz to start walking. The most common plan is two days and one night: sleep at the campsite on the first day, climb to the summit at dawn on the second, and descend by the same trail. On a clear day Mount Banahaw, Mount Isarog and Mayon Volcano may be visible from the top, but clouds are common, so the view is a matter of luck. The area is said to be home to rafflesia and hornbills, so the mountain suits people who enjoy the forest itself.

Before you go, keep in mind that this mountain is not set up like a tourist attraction. There is no published official entrance fee or price list, and guiding and camping depend heavily on villagers and local mountaineering groups. In return you get quiet, natural forest, but you must organize everything yourself. If your schedule is tight, it is safer to book two nights in Daet, one for travel and preparation and one for the climb. Travelers are best off going in a group of four or five to share the jeepney and guide costs, and agreeing with the guide or a porter on how to split heavy loads. People who have done it say the trail is long and humid, but the reward of camping in a silent jungle is great.

blocks.title: Summit of the highest peak in Camarines Norte

children.text: The summit is about 1,544 m above sea level. You set out from the campsite before dawn and climb for two to three hours through thickly mossy forest and rocky ridges. When the clouds clear, you may see toward Mayon Volcano and Mount Isarog.

About 13 km from the start to the campsite follows an old road built for geothermal exploration. It passes rice fields and farmland and gradually enters the forest, and because the road is wide, it is relatively easy walking before the second day. Some stretches are overgrown with little shade, so protect yourself from the sun.

You cross rivers three to five times before reaching the campsite. The first is a ford about 4 km from the start. The last river has to be waded and its rocks are slippery. Water can rise suddenly in the rain, so follow your guide's judgment.
About 1 km from the campsite, a descent of
15–30 minutes
on foot brings you to Angelina Falls. This waterfall hidden in the forest is a good place to wash off sweat and refill water. Most groups visit on the afternoon they arrive.

Rafflesia manillana and hornbills are said to live around Mount Labo. Rafflesia usually blooms for a week or two in June or July, so ask a local guide about timing and location. In the mossy forest you can see pitcher plants, butterflies and many insects.

blocks.title: A small campsite for one group

children.text: The campsite is near an old geothermal drill site at about 800 m above sea level and is small. The dense forest makes nights quiet and cool. Some trip reports mention bees gathering around headlamps in the early morning.

blocks.title: Finish at Bagasbas Beach in Daet

children.text: After coming down, many people return to Daet and wash up and relax at Bagasbas Beach. The beach is famous for surfing, so watching the waves and having a meal there is a good way to end the day.

items.title: Standard 2-day, 1-night route
items.subtitle: One night at the campsite, summit push at dawn

children.text: Your group arrives at the Daet terminal after the night bus from Manila. Have breakfast and buy snacks, water and food.
Ride a rented jeepney or tricycle to San Isidro, which takes about
1 hour
. Sign the logbook at the barangay hall and meet your guide.
Start the trek. After about 4 km along the old road you reach the first river, then cross several more.
Eat lunch near the second river and check the condition of your shoes and socks.
Arrive at the campsite and pitch your tent. You have walked about 13 km and climbed about 700 m. If time remains, visit Angelina Falls.
Eat dinner and go to bed early. Save your energy for the dawn start.
Arrival times differ between trip reports. A fast team reached the campsite in about
3.5 hours
, while a slow one takes
6 hours
or more.

items.title: Day two: summit and descent
items.subtitle: Dawn start, down by the afternoon

children.text: Wake up, eat a light meal and get ready with only a light pack.
Start the summit push. Climb the steep mossy forest trail, and refill water at the two brooks about halfway up.
Reach the summit. If there are no clouds, you can see distant volcanoes.
Return to the campsite, pack up, and eat breakfast or an early lunch.
Walk back down to the trailhead. The descent takes as long as the climb, so allow plenty of time. Then head to Daet for a bus or your hotel.
Take a Daet-bound bus (Philtranco, DLTB and others) from the Pasay or Cubao terminal. The trip takes about
9 hours
, and many buses leave around
as night buses.
Per 2026 booking portals, a regular air-conditioned bus costs about
(the ₱550 in a 2013 trip report is outdated). Fares change often, so check at the terminal.
You can also stay a night in Daet and start the next morning.

items.title: From Daet to the trailhead village

children.text: San Isidro (San Lorenzo Ruiz) is about
1 hour
away. Regular jeepneys are rare, so many people charter a jeepney or take a tricycle.
In past trip reports, chartering a jeepney cost about
one way or about
round trip. Ask your guide for the current price.
There are domestic flights from Manila to Naga Airport (WNP). From Naga to Daet you travel by bus or van. Routes change often, so check the latest schedules.
Labo gets a lot of rain through the year and is a jungle trek, so it is more comfortable in the dry season. When it rains, the rivers can rise quickly and become hard to cross, and leeches multiply.
If you want to see rafflesia, it is generally said to bloom for a week or two in June or July, but timing varies by year, so ask a local guide.

There is no lodging or restaurant on the mountain, so you sleep in a tent at the campsite and eat the food you carry. Some trip reports mention a last water source near the camp, but it is safer to boil or filter any water you drink. Before you start, buy rice, canned food, snacks and spare socks at the Daet market or a supermarket.

Daet is the base before and after the trek. There are many hotels and restaurants around the terminal and in town, and near Bagasbas Beach there are cafes and lodging popular with surfers. A late descent can make you miss the bus to Manila, so we recommend spending a night in Daet.

The campsite fits only about one group, so a large party should agree on numbers with the guide in advance. Bring a reliably waterproof tent, plus spare shoes and plastic bags for wet footwear. For breakfast, something that cooks fast, such as instant noodles or porridge, is convenient.
Guides from local mountaineering clubs (such as ORYOL) look after the trail. Before you leave, confirm a guide's contact through the local tourism office or trip reports.
Always sign the logbook at the barangay hall in San Isidro before you start. Rules and fees can change, so check the latest information.
Bring long socks, gaiters, and salt or repellent against leeches (limatik). They are especially numerous after rain.
You cross rivers many times, so you need spare socks and shoes and waterproof pouches. Keep wet and dry clothes separate.
A headlamp is essential for the dawn summit push, and bees may gather around lights at the campsite, so avoid walking with your light on at camp.
Some trip reports say mobile signal is available almost to the summit, but it is not guaranteed. Bring a power bank and a paper map.
A day hike is said to take about
10–12 hours
round trip, but it is very hard. We recommend it only for very fit, experienced hikers.
Carry out all your trash and do not collect wild plants.
Rain can make the rivers rise sharply, so do not cross when the water is up and follow your guide's judgment. Leave slack in your schedule.
This is a volcanic area, so check the latest PHIVOLCS advisories. It is currently a potentially active volcano with no eruption on record in recent times.
Mossy rocks and steep loose landslide sections are easy to slip on. On stretches without a rope, help one another down.
You may meet snakes and insects on the mountain. Do not touch them with bare hands.
The trail is faint in places, so you can get lost without a guide.
Recent information is limited, so confirm trail conditions with the village and your guide before you go.
A surf beach near Daet, a good place to relax about
20–30 minutes
away after the descent.
The main city of Camarines Norte and the base for the trek, with a terminal, lodging and restaurants.
A remote island resort reached by boat from the Camarines Norte coast, which you can add as a beach stop after the climb.
The signature volcano of the Bicol region, said to be visible in the direction from Labo's summit on a clear day.
